name: Cucumber Mint Water
flavorProfile: Cool and faintly green, with mint and lime lifting plain water without sweetening it.
healthBenefit: Plain water with enough flavor that it gets drunk. No sugar, and a little potassium from the cucumber.
instructions: Put the cucumber, mint and lime slices in a jug and pour the water over them.
Chill for at least an hour so the flavors move into the water.
Drink within a day. The cucumber goes soft after that.

name: Strawberry Lemon Water
flavorProfile: Lightly fruity and tart, with the strawberries coloring the water pink as they sit.
healthBenefit: A way to drink more water that carries almost none of the sugar of a fruit juice, since the berries flavor it rather than being blended into it.
instructions: Put the halved strawberries and lemon slices in a jug and press them once or twice with a spoon to release a little juice.
Pour the water over and chill for at least an hour.
Eat the strawberries once the water is gone.

name: Warm Lemon Ginger Water
flavorProfile: Warm and sharp, with the ginger heat building as it steeps and the honey rounding the lemon.
healthBenefit: Ginger is one of the better-studied plant remedies for nausea, and a warm drink first thing tends to get drunk when a cold glass of water does not.
instructions: Heat the water until it is steaming but not boiling.
Drop in the ginger slices and let them steep for 5 minutes.
Stir in the lemon juice and honey once the water is cool enough to drink.

name: Chamomile Tea with Honey and Lemon
flavorProfile: Soft and apple-like, with a little honey and a squeeze of lemon on top.
healthBenefit: Caffeine-free, so it suits the last hour of the day. Chamomile has a small body of trial evidence for sleep and mild anxiety, most of it short and small.
instructions: Steep a chamomile tea bag, or 1 teaspoon dried chamomile flowers, in 250ml of just-boiled water for 5 minutes with a saucer over the cup.
Take out the bag or strain out the flowers.
When the tea is cool enough to drink, stir in the honey and squeeze in the lemon.

name: Rooibos Cinnamon Latte
flavorProfile: Rounded and slightly sweet, with the red tea tasting almost of vanilla under the warm milk.
healthBenefit: A caffeine-free latte. Rooibos brews strong without the tannin bitterness black tea gets, so it stands up to milk without sugar doing the work.

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: Brew two rooibos tea bags in 120ml of boiling water for 7 to 10 minutes, so the tea is strong enough to taste through the milk.
Remove the tea bags and stir in the maple syrup while the tea is hot.
Heat the milk in a small pan until it steams but does not boil, whisking to froth it.
Pour the milk over the tea and dust the cinnamon on top.

name: Hibiscus Lime Iced Tea
flavorProfile: Deep red, tart like cranberry, with lime sharpening it and honey taking the edge off.
healthBenefit: Hibiscus has several small trials behind a modest blood pressure reduction. A tablespoon of honey sweetens the whole jug, so you know exactly how much sugar each glass carries.
instructions: Steep 7.5 g (about 2 tablespoons) dried hibiscus, or one hibiscus tea bag, in 500ml of boiling water for 10 minutes.
Strain, and stir in the honey while the tea is still warm so it dissolves.
Chill, then stir in the lime juice and serve over ice.

name: Peach Iced Black Tea
flavorProfile: Brisk black tea with ripe peach and mint steeped in, a little honey, and plenty of lemon.
healthBenefit: The peach slices and mint steep in the warm tea as it cools, and a small spoon of honey stirred in while hot rounds out the lemon. Brewed black tea carries polyphenols and about half the caffeine of coffee.
instructions: Brew two black tea bags in 500ml of boiling water for 4 minutes and remove them, so the tea does not turn bitter.
Stir the honey into the hot tea until it dissolves, then drop in the peach slices and mint leaves and leave it to cool on the counter.
Chill for 2 hours, add the lemon juice, and serve over ice with the peach slices left in.

name: Homemade Chai
flavorProfile: Warm and spiced, with ginger heat, cardamom and clove behind strong black tea and milk.
healthBenefit: Made at home, a cup of chai carries about two teaspoons of honey. The coffee-shop version is built on a syrup concentrate that puts it closer to a dessert.

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: Put 60ml of water in a small pan with the ginger, cinnamon, cardamom and cloves and simmer 2 to 3 minutes.
Add a black tea bag, or 1 tablespoon loose black tea, and simmer 1 minute more.
Pour in the milk and heat until it is about to boil, then turn the heat down and simmer 2 minutes.
Strain into a mug and stir in the honey.

name: Cinnamon Cardamom Coffee
flavorProfile: Ordinary drip coffee with a warm, faintly floral edge from spices brewed in with the grounds.
healthBenefit: The spices go into the filter, so the flavor comes through without any syrup. A splash of milk is the only thing added to the cup.

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: Stir the cinnamon and cardamom into the ground coffee before brewing, so they brew through with it.
Brew as you normally would, by drip, pour-over or press.
Add the milk to the cup.

name: Stovetop Hot Cocoa
flavorProfile: Dark and chocolatey with a hint of cinnamon, made from plain cocoa powder and sweetened with maple syrup.
healthBenefit: Unsweetened cocoa is one of the denser sources of flavanols, and making it from powder means you can see exactly what sweetens it: three tablespoons of maple syrup here, which you can reduce to taste.

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: Whisk the cocoa and cinnamon with a splash of the milk in a small pan until there are no lumps.
Add the rest of the milk and the maple syrup and warm over medium-low heat, whisking, until steaming.
Do not let it boil. Pour into a cup.

name: Stovetop Apple Cider
flavorProfile: Warm, sweet and spiced, tasting of the apples themselves rather than of a concentrate.
healthBenefit: Made from whole apples and a little orange simmered and pressed, it keeps some of the apple pectin that a filtered juice loses, with a little brown sugar stirred in.
instructions: Put the quartered apples and orange, the water, cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg in a pan and bring to a simmer.
Simmer, covered, for 30 minutes, until the apples have collapsed.
Mash the fruit in the pan, then strain through a sieve, pressing to get the liquid out.
Stir in the brown sugar until it dissolves and serve warm.

name: Cranberry Orange Cooler
flavorProfile: Tart and bright, with orange juice softening the cranberry bite.
healthBenefit: Bottled cranberry drinks are mostly sugar water because the fruit is so sour. Simmering whole berries and sweetening with a measured amount of maple syrup keeps the fruit and lets you see exactly how much sugar goes in.
instructions: Simmer the cranberries in the water about 10 minutes, until every berry has burst.
Strain through a sieve, pressing the berries to get the liquid out, and stir in the maple syrup while it is warm.
Chill, then stir in the orange juice and serve over ice.

name: Tart Cherry Cooler
flavorProfile: Sour and deep, with lime and honey rounding it into something you want a second glass of.
healthBenefit: Sour cherries are the variety studied for muscle recovery and sleep, in small trials using concentrated juice. Here the whole fruit is simmered with honey into a concentrate, then topped with cold water and ice.
instructions: Put the cherries and honey in a small saucepan over medium-high heat and bring to a boil. Lower the heat and simmer for 15 to 20 minutes, then let it cool.
Stir in the lime juice. This is the concentrate.
Divide the concentrate between two tall glasses, fill with ice and top with the cold water. Stir before drinking.
Concentrate keeps up to ten days in a glass jar in the refrigerator.

name: Cantaloupe Lime Agua Fresca
flavorProfile: Light, sweet and melon-forward, thinned with water so it drinks like a cooler rather than a smoothie.
healthBenefit: Cantaloupe is one of the highest vitamin A fruits, and blending it with water rather than juicing it keeps the fiber in the glass.
instructions: Blend the cantaloupe, water, lime juice and honey until smooth.
Taste. A ripe melon may not need the honey at all.
Serve over ice. Stir before pouring if it has separated.

name: Blueberry Lemonade
flavorProfile: Tart lemonade turned purple by whole blueberries, sweetened with a measured spoonful of maple syrup and strained smooth.
healthBenefit: Making lemonade at home means you set the sugar: here it is one and a half tablespoons of maple syrup alongside the natural sweetness of the blueberries, which also add their anthocyanins.
instructions: Put the blueberries, water, lemon juice, maple syrup and salt in a blender and blend on high 30 to 60 seconds, until smooth.
Pour through a fine sieve to catch the skins.
Serve over ice.

name: Pineapple Ginger Juice
flavorProfile: Sweet, tropical and hot at the back, with lime holding the pineapple sugar in check.
healthBenefit: Fresh pineapple carries bromelain, an enzyme that a pasteurized juice has lost, along with a full day of vitamin C in a glass. Blending and lightly straining keeps more fiber than a juicer would.
instructions: Blend the pineapple, ginger, lime juice and water until smooth.
Strain through a coarse sieve if you want it thinner, or drink it as it is.
Serve cold.

name: Carrot Orange Ginger Juice
flavorProfile: Sweet and earthy from the carrot, bright from the orange, with a ginger kick.
healthBenefit: Two vegetables-worth of beta-carotene in a glass, and the orange supplies the vitamin C. No juicer needed: a blender and a sieve do it.
instructions: Blend the carrot, orange, ginger and water on high for a full minute, until the carrot is completely broken down.
Strain through a fine sieve, pressing the pulp with the back of a spoon.
Serve cold. Stir before drinking.

name: Beet Apple Lemon Juice
flavorProfile: Earthy and sweet, deep magenta, with lemon keeping the beet from tasting like soil.
healthBenefit: Beets are the food source of dietary nitrate that trials have tied to lower blood pressure and better exercise endurance. The apple sweetens it without any added sugar.
instructions: Blend the beet, apple, lemon juice and water on high for a full minute.
Strain through a fine sieve, pressing the pulp.
Serve cold. Beet stains, so rinse the blender straight away.

name: Homemade Oat Milk
flavorProfile: Mild, faintly sweet and creamy, with none of the gums or oils a carton version carries.
healthBenefit: Oats and water, plus two dates and a pinch of salt. Carton oat milk is usually made with added oil, and often with sugar released by enzymes. This has neither.
instructions: Blend the oats, cold water, dates and salt for about 30 seconds and no longer, since longer blending makes oat milk slimy.
Pour through a fine sieve or a cloth into a jar without pressing the pulp.
Keep in the fridge up to 4 days and shake before pouring, since it separates.

name: Mango Lassi
flavorProfile: Thick, cold and sweet, with cardamom giving the mango a floral edge.
healthBenefit: Greek yogurt gives this the protein a fruit juice lacks, so it holds you between meals. The mango and a tablespoon of honey do the sweetening.

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: Blend the mango, yogurt, milk, honey and cardamom until smooth.
Add a splash more milk if it is too thick to pour.
Serve cold.

name: Lemon Mustard Vinaigrette
flavorProfile: Sharp and clean, with the mustard holding the oil and lemon together so it coats rather than puddles.
healthBenefit: A bottled dressing lists sugar, thickeners and refined oil; this is olive oil and lemon. The oil helps the fat-soluble vitamins in whatever you pour it over absorb.
instructions: Put the lemon juice, olive oil, Dijon mustard, salt and pepper in a small jar with a tight lid.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds, until it is combined and slightly thick.
Keeps for up to a week. Shake again before each use.

name: Orange Ginger Dressing
flavorProfile: Sweet and citrusy with a ginger bite, lighter than a vinaigrette because orange juice makes up most of it.
healthBenefit: The orange juice replaces vinegar, which matters if vinegar bothers your stomach, and it carries the sweetness so no sugar is added.
instructions: Stir the salt into the orange juice until it dissolves, then add the orange zest, ginger and pepper.
Add the olive oil and shake hard in a closed jar for about 30 seconds, or whisk until it comes together.
Keeps up to 7 days in the refrigerator. Shake again before using.

name: Carrot Ginger Dressing
flavorProfile: Bright orange, sweet and gingery, thick enough to cling to a salad the way the Japanese restaurant version does.
healthBenefit: A whole carrot blended into the dressing, so the beta-carotene comes with the oil that helps it absorb.
instructions: Put the carrot, olive oil, rice vinegar, ginger, lemon zest, lemon juice, maple syrup, sesame oil and salt in a blender.
Blend on high until smooth, scraping down the sides once.
Taste and add a little more lemon juice or salt if you like. Keeps refrigerated for 5 days.

name: Yogurt Ranch Dressing
flavorProfile: Cool, herby and tangy, with the dill and garlic doing what the packet does without the powder.
healthBenefit: Greek yogurt in place of the mayonnaise and buttermilk base, which swaps most of the fat for protein and adds live cultures.

ingredients.prepNote: to thin, a tablespoon at a time

instructions: Whisk the yogurt, garlic, chives, dill, vinegar, lemon juice, salt and pepper until smooth, or blend for a smoother dressing.
Refrigerate in a covered container for at least 30 minutes, or overnight.
To pour it over salad, thin with the water a tablespoon at a time.

name: Ginger Lime Marinade
flavorProfile: Sharp, hot and a little sweet, for chicken, fish, tofu or vegetables headed for the grill.
healthBenefit: Enough acid and oil to season about 700g of protein or vegetables, without the soy sauce a bottled marinade is built on and with only a spoonful of maple syrup.
instructions: Whisk the lime juice, grated ginger, olive oil, maple syrup, salt and pepper together in a bowl.
Pour it over about 700g of salmon or other fish, chicken, tofu or sliced vegetables and turn to coat.
Marinate in the fridge for 30 to 60 minutes (no more than 6 hours for fish), then cook. Discard what the raw food sat in.

name: Lemon Garlic Herb Marinade
flavorProfile: Lemony and green, with garlic and fresh herbs, for chicken, fish or vegetables.
healthBenefit: Marinating in lemon and olive oil before grilling has been shown to reduce the formation of heterocyclic amines, the compounds that form when meat chars.
instructions: Whisk the lemon zest, lemon juice, olive oil, garlic, parsley, dill, salt and pepper together in a bowl.
Pour it over about 450g of fish or chicken and turn to coat.
Marinate in the fridge, fish for 20 to 30 minutes and chicken for 30 minutes to 2 hours, then cook. Discard what the raw food sat in.

name: Tzatziki
flavorProfile: Cold, thick and garlicky, with grated cucumber and dill through it.
healthBenefit: Mostly Greek yogurt and cucumber, so it carries protein and live cultures where a mayonnaise-based dip carries fat. Squeezing the cucumber is what keeps it thick.
instructions: Put the yogurt, cucumber, garlic, dill, lemon juice, olive oil and salt in a bowl and whisk until combined.
Keeps refrigerated for 3 days.

name: Cucumber Mint Raita
flavorProfile: Cool and mild, with mint and toasted cumin, made to sit beside something hot and spiced.
healthBenefit: The cooling side dish of Indian cooking, and the reason a spiced meal is easier on the stomach. Yogurt protein and cucumber water, nothing else to speak of.
instructions: If your cumin is not already roasted, toast the ground cumin in a dry pan for about 30 seconds, until it smells toasty, and let it cool.
Stir the yogurt until smooth.
Fold in the cucumber, mint, salt, cumin and pepper.
Chill before serving, and eat it the same day.

name: Avocado Lime Sauce
flavorProfile: Smooth, green and tangy, a creamy sauce for tacos, bowls or grilled fish.
healthBenefit: Avocado supplies the creaminess with monounsaturated fat and potassium, and Greek yogurt and lime make it tangy without any oil.
instructions: Put the avocado, yogurt, lime juice, salt and cilantro in a food processor or blender.
Blend for 30 to 60 seconds, until smooth and creamy.
Use the same day. It browns at the surface after that, though it is still fine underneath.

name: Tahini Ginger Sauce
flavorProfile: Nutty, sharp and a little sweet, the sauce a grain bowl or a tray of roasted vegetables usually gets from peanuts.
healthBenefit: Sesame in place of peanuts, so it is safe for a peanut allergy and brings calcium and magnesium along with the fat.

ingredients.prepNote: a little at a time, until pourable

instructions: Whisk the tahini, lemon juice, maple syrup, salt and ginger together. It will seize and thicken; keep stirring.
Add the water a little at a time until the sauce pours easily.
Taste and add more lemon, maple syrup, ginger or salt if you like. Keeps covered in the refrigerator for up to a week.

name: Fresh Tomato Salsa
flavorProfile: Chunky, juicy and sharp, with raw onion, cilantro and lime.
healthBenefit: Raw tomato, onion and lime, with the salt in your control. Jarred salsa can carry more sodium per serving than a bag of chips.
instructions: Put the finely diced onion in a strainer and rinse it under cold water, then shake off the water.
Combine the tomato, onion, serrano chile and cilantro in a bowl.
Stir in the lime juice and the salt, then taste and add a little more salt if it needs it.
Let it stand for about an hour if you can, when the flavor is at its best, and serve at room temperature. Best the same day; drain off any extra liquid if it sits longer.

name: Mango Salsa
flavorProfile: Sweet, sharp and crunchy, with red pepper and lime against ripe mango.
healthBenefit: A fruit salsa that brings vitamin C from both the mango and the pepper, and turns plain grilled fish or chicken into a meal without a sauce.
instructions: Combine the mango, red pepper, red onion, cilantro, garlic, jalapeño, lime juice and salt in a bowl and stir.
Taste and add a little more salt if it needs it.
Chill until you serve it. Best the same day.

name: Parsley Garlic Chimichurri
flavorProfile: Green, garlicky and sharp, loose enough to spoon over grilled meat or roasted vegetables.
healthBenefit: A whole bunch of parsley goes into a small batch, which makes this one of the few sauces that counts as a serving of leafy greens. Lemon stands in for the usual vinegar.
instructions: Stir the parsley, oregano, garlic, jalapeño, salt and pepper together in a bowl.
Stir in the olive oil and lemon juice. It should be loose and spoonable, not a paste.
Let it sit for 30 minutes before serving. Keeps refrigerated for up to 2 days.

name: Roasted Tomato Garlic Sauce
flavorProfile: Deeper and sweeter than a stovetop tomato sauce, with the garlic gone soft and mellow in the oven.
healthBenefit: Roasting concentrates the tomatoes and makes their lycopene more available than it is raw, and the olive oil they roast in helps it absorb.
instructions: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C).

Toss the tomato halves with the olive oil and lay them cut side down on a rimmed baking sheet. Add the garlic cloves in their skins, sprinkle with the salt, and tuck the thyme sprigs among the tomatoes.
Roast for about 45 minutes, until the skins shrivel and the tomatoes release their juice.
Let them cool a little. Pull off the tomato skins, lift out the thyme sprigs, and squeeze the garlic out of its skins.
Blend the tomatoes and garlic to the texture you like. For a thicker sauce, simmer it in a pan until it thickens. Keeps 3 days refrigerated or up to a year frozen.

name: Roasted Red Pepper Sauce
flavorProfile: Smoky-sweet and smooth, the color of paprika, good on eggs, grains, fish or pasta.
healthBenefit: Red bell peppers carry more vitamin C by weight than oranges, and roasting them adds sweetness with no sugar.
instructions: Roast the peppers over a gas flame, or under a hot broiler on a foil-lined sheet, turning them until blackened all over.
Put them in a covered bowl or a closed paper bag for about 20 minutes.
Peel off the skins and take out the seeds. Do not rinse them, which washes away flavor.
Blend the peppers with the garlic, olive oil, lemon juice, salt and pepper until smooth. Keeps refrigerated for 5 days.

name: Coconut Ginger Sauce
flavorProfile: Rich, creamy and gently spiced with ginger and garlic, a quick sauce for vegetables, fish or chickpeas.
healthBenefit: Coconut milk gives it body without cream or flour, and fresh ginger brings one of the anti-inflammatory spices that trials have looked at.
instructions: Warm the coconut oil in a small pan over medium heat and let the garlic sizzle for a few seconds.
Add the ginger and cook for 1 minute, stirring.
Pour in the coconut milk, then add the lime juice, salt and pepper.
Bring it to a boil, then turn the heat down and simmer for 1 minute.

name: Onion Gravy
flavorProfile: Dark, sweet from slow-cooked onions, and thick enough to pour over mash or roasted vegetables.
healthBenefit: Built on slowly browned onions and vegetable stock rather than meat drippings and flour, so it is gluten-free and carries a fraction of the saturated fat.
instructions: Heat the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring now and then, until deeply browned.
Add the garlic, rosemary, thyme, sage and pepper and stir for 2 minutes.
Pour in the stock and tamari and simmer for 10 minutes.
Whisk the arrowroot into the cold water until smooth, then stir it into the pan. Cook gently for about 3 minutes, stirring, until it thickens. Do not boil it hard, which thins arrowroot back out.

name: Unsweetened Applesauce
flavorProfile: Soft, warm and tasting of apples and cinnamon, with a little lemon keeping it bright.
healthBenefit: Jarred applesauce is often sweetened; this one takes all its sugar from the fruit and keeps the pectin, a soluble fiber that gut bacteria feed on.
instructions: Put the apples, water, lemon juice and cinnamon in a pan. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer for 10 to 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the apples are soft enough to pierce easily with a fork.
Mash with a potato masher or fork for a chunky sauce, or blend for a smooth one.
Keeps refrigerated for a week, or freeze it for longer.

name: Cranberry Orange Sauce
flavorProfile: Tart, jammy and bright with orange, for roast poultry, a grain bowl or stirred into yogurt.
healthBenefit: The canned version is around a third sugar by weight. Here the maple syrup adds much less than that, and the whole berries and orange do the rest.

ingredients.prepNote: zest of about ½ orange, cooked in with the berries
in place of the cinnamon stick

instructions: Rinse the cranberries and pick out any soft ones and stems.
Put the cranberries, maple syrup, orange zest, orange juice, water and cinnamon in a saucepan over medium heat. Stir now and then until it boils.
Keep it boiling for 15 to 20 minutes, until the berries burst and it forms a sauce.
Taste, and if it is too tart add a little more maple syrup. Take it off the heat and let it cool; it thickens as it cools.
Keep it in a closed container in the refrigerator for 3 to 4 days, or freeze it for up to 2 months.

name: Blueberry Maple Sauce
flavorProfile: Warm, glossy and purple, with whole berries in a light syrup, for pancakes, oatmeal or yogurt.
healthBenefit: Two tablespoons of maple syrup go into the batch, so each serving carries some added sugar next to the berries.
instructions: Put half the blueberries in a small pan with the maple syrup, water and lemon juice. Simmer over medium heat for about 10 minutes, stirring now and then.
Add the rest of the blueberries and cook about 8 minutes more, stirring occasionally.
Take it off the heat and let it rest a few minutes; it thickens as it cools. Keeps refrigerated for 5 days.
